title: Fasting Blood Sugar
path: Management of Clients with Problems of the Metabolic and Endocrine System

headings.title: Introduction to Fasting Blood Sugar
headings.content: Fasting blood sugar, often abbreviated as FBS, measures the amount of glucose circulating in the bloodstream after an extended period of food abstinence. This laboratory investigation serves as a primary tool for screening and diagnosing metabolic disorders like diabetes mellitus. Unlike random blood glucose testing, the fasting parameter eliminates the immediate postprandial glycemic surge, offering a stable baseline of carbohydrate metabolism. In clinical practice across Nigeria, rising numbers of undiagnosed type 2 diabetes cases make routine FBS screening vital during general medical checkups.

headings.title: Physiology of Glucose Regulation
headings.content: Blood glucose homeostasis depends on a delicate hormonal balance, primarily involving insulin and glucagon secreted by the pancreas. When an individual fasts, falling blood glucose levels trigger a decrease in insulin release and an increase in glucagon secretion. Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis, breaking down stored glycogen into glucose to maintain normal plasma concentrations. If the fast continues, the liver initiates gluconeogenesis, synthesizing new glucose from amino acids and glycerol. Impairment in this feedback loop leads to pathological hyperglycemia characteristic of diabetes.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Purpose
headings.content:
Healthcare providers order fasting blood sugar tests for multiple clinical scenarios. 

- **Diagnosis**: Primary screening tool for individuals presenting with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia like polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss.
- **Monitoring**: Evaluating the therapeutic efficacy of oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin therapy in known diabetic patients.
- **Risk Assessment**: Screening high-risk populations, including pregnant women for gestational diabetes, patients with hypertension, or those with a strong family history of metabolic syndrome.

headings.title: Pre-Test Preparation and Instructions
headings.content:
Accurate test results rely heavily on strict adherence to pre-test preparation. Nurses must instruct patients to fast for a minimum of eight to twelve hours prior to blood sample collection. During this fasting window, patients may consume water, but they must avoid tea, coffee, alcohol, and sugary drinks. 

A common misconception is that chewing sugar-free gum or taking morning routine medications has no impact; however, nurses must review all drug charts because corticosteroids, diuretics, and certain beta-blockers can artificially elevate glucose readings. Strenuous physical exercise should also be avoided the night before testing.

headings.title: Reference Ranges and Clinical Interpretation
headings.content:
Laboratory interpretation of fasting blood sugar relies on standardized numerical cutoffs established by international health organizations.

| Classification | Fasting Plasma Glucose Range (mg/dL) |
| --- | --- |
| Normal | Less than 100 mg/dL |
| Prediabetes | 100 to 125 mg/dL |
| Provisional Diabetes Diagnosis | 126 mg/dL or higher on two separate tests |

Values falling within the prediabetic range warn of impending metabolic dysfunction, giving patients an opportunity for lifestyle modification.

headings.title: Factors Affecting Accuracy
headings.content: Several physiological and external variables can distort fasting blood sugar results, leading to misdiagnosis. Acute stress, trauma, or recent surgical procedures trigger counter-regulatory hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which spike blood glucose. Conversely, prolonged fasting beyond twenty-four hours can sometimes cause unexpected metabolic shifts. Additionally, severe hemolysis in the collected blood sample or delayed transport to the laboratory can falsely lower glucose measurements as red blood cells continue to metabolize sugar in the vial.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Patient Education
headings.content: Nurses act as the critical bridge between the laboratory and the patient. Responsibilities begin with verifying fasting compliance before sample collection and ensuring correct specimen labeling. Following the procedure, the nurse must monitor the venipuncture site for hematoma formation and provide light refreshments if the patient feels dizzy. Education involves explaining dietary modifications, physical activity guidelines, and the importance of keeping follow-up appointments to review laboratory outcomes.
